title: Appealing a decision
intro: This guide describes, in general terms, which Ontario court hears an appeal and how the court rules say an appeal is started. It explains what the law and rules say; it does not say whether any particular decision can or should be appealed.

sections.heading: Which court hears an appeal
paragraphs: The Courts of Justice Act says “An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from,” among other things, “a final order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice, as described in subsections (1.1) and (1.2)” and “an interlocutory order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice, with leave as provided in the rules of court”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1))

If the notice of appeal is filed on or after October 1, 2007, the final orders that go to the Divisional Court include an order “for a single payment of not more than $50,000, exclusive of costs” and an order “dismissing a claim for an amount that is not more than the amount set out in clause (a) or (b)”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1.2))

An appeal lies to the Court of Appeal from “a final order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice”, with exceptions, including the orders that go to the Divisional Court under section 19. An order of the Divisional Court can be appealed to the Court of Appeal “on a question that is not a question of fact alone, with leave of the Court of Appeal as provided in the rules of court”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1))
Leave of the Court of Appeal is not required for a Divisional Court order on an appeal under Part V or VIII of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1.0.1))

“Unless otherwise provided”, a court hearing an appeal may “make any order or decision that ought to or could have been made by the court or tribunal appealed from”, may “order a new trial”, or may “make any other order or decision that is considered just”. The Act also says “A judge shall not sit as a member of a court hearing an appeal from his or her own decision.” (Courts of Justice Act, ss. 132, 134 (1))

sections.heading: Appeals from Small Claims Court
paragraphs: The Courts of Justice Act says “An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from a final order of the Small Claims Court in an action,” either “for the payment of money in excess of the prescribed amount, excluding costs” or “for the recovery of possession of personal property exceeding the prescribed amount in value”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 31)
A regulation sets the “prescribed amount”. For both clauses of section 31, “the prescribed amount is $5,000.” (O. Reg. 626/00, s. 2)

The ontario.ca guide puts it this way: a judgment can be appealed to a higher court “if the amount of the judgment, not including court costs, is more than $5,000, or there is an order directing recovery of personal property valued at more than $5,000.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)

The same guide says an appeal “is not an opportunity to retell your story.” It also says “The judge who hears the appeal will not hear any new evidence; they will rely entirely on the transcript of the trial and the court record.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)

The Courts of Justice Act, however, says that unless otherwise provided, a court to which an appeal is taken may, “in a proper case”, “receive further evidence by affidavit, transcript of oral examination, oral examination before the court or in such other manner as the court directs”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 134 (4) (b))

A proceeding in the Divisional Court “shall be heard and determined by three judges sitting together”. But it “may be heard and determined by one judge” where it is “an appeal under section 31 from a person referred to in subsection 24 (2) presiding over the Small Claims Court”. The persons referred to in subsection 24 (2) are a deputy judge and the Small Claims Court Administrative Judge. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 21 (1), (2), s. 24 (2))

In the Rules of Civil Procedure, “appellate court” means “the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court, as the circumstances require”. Rules 61.02 to 61.16 apply “to all appeals to an appellate court”, with some listed exceptions. The steps for starting an appeal under Rule 61 are described in the civil section of this guide. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 1.03 (1), r. 61.01)

sections.heading: Leave to appeal
paragraphs: Some appeals can only go ahead with “leave” of the appeal court. The Courts of Justice Act says “No appeal lies without leave of the court to which the appeal is to be taken,” from “an order made with the consent of the parties” or “where the appeal is only as to costs that are in the discretion of the court that made the order for costs.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 133)

Leave to appeal to the Divisional Court from “An interlocutory order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice” is obtained from a panel of that court. The motion for leave “shall be heard in writing, without the attendance of parties or lawyers.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.02 (1), (2))

Leave to appeal from an interlocutory order “shall not be granted unless” there is “a conflicting decision by another judge or court in Ontario or elsewhere on the matter involved in the proposed appeal” and the panel considers leave desirable, or there appears to the panel “good reason to doubt the correctness of the order in question” and the proposed appeal “involves matters of such importance that, in the panel's opinion, leave to appeal should be granted”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.02 (4))

A notice of motion for leave to appeal to the Divisional Court is to be served “within 15 days after the making of the order or decision from which leave to appeal is sought, unless a statute provides otherwise”, and filed with proof of service “within five days after service”. The same 15-day and five-day times apply to a motion for leave from an interlocutory order under rule 62.02. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03 (1), r. 61.03.1 (3), r. 62.02 (3))

Where the Court of Appeal's leave is required, the motion “shall be heard in writing, without the attendance of parties or lawyers”, and the notice of motion has the same 15-day service and five-day filing times. If the court decides an oral hearing is warranted, it orders one. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03.1 (1), (3), (15))

In both courts, “Where leave is granted, the notice of appeal shall be delivered within seven days after the granting of leave.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03 (6), r. 61.03.1 (16), r. 62.02 (8))

sections.heading: Starting an appeal in a civil case
paragraphs: An appeal to the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court starts by serving a notice of appeal in Form 61A.2 (Court of Appeal) or 61A.3 (Divisional Court), with a certificate respecting evidence, “within 30 days after the making of the order appealed from, unless a statute or these rules provide otherwise”. It is served on “every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal” and on “any person entitled by statute to be heard on the appeal”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (1))

It need not be served on a defendant who was noted in default, or on a respondent who has not delivered a notice of appearance unless that respondent was heard at the hearing with leave. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (1.1))

The notice of appeal states “the relief sought”, “the grounds of appeal”, and the basis for the appeal court's jurisdiction, including whether the order is final or interlocutory and whether leave is needed. It is filed with proof of service “within ten days after service”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (3), (4))

With the notice of appeal, the appellant serves and files a certificate (Form 61C) “setting out only the portions of the evidence that, in the appellant's opinion, are required for the appeal.” Instead, the parties may, within thirty days after service of the notice of appeal, make an agreement about the documents and transcript required for the appeal. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.05 (1), (4))

Within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal, the appellant files proof of having ordered a transcript of all oral evidence that the parties have not agreed to omit. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.05 (5))

The appellant “perfects” the appeal by serving and filing the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and a factum. This is due “within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal” if no transcript is needed, or “within 60 days after receiving notice that the evidence has been transcribed” if one is. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.09 (1), (3))

“No grounds other than those stated in the notice of appeal or cross-appeal or supplementary notice may be relied on at the hearing, except with leave of the court hearing the appeal.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.08 (2))

A different procedure, in rule 62.01, applies to an appeal made to a judge, such as an appeal to the Superior Court of Justice from “an interlocutory order of a master, case management master or associate judge”. That appeal starts by serving a notice of appeal (Form 62A) “within seven days after the making of the order or certificate appealed from.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 17; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.01 (1), (2))

sections.heading: What happens to the order during an appeal
paragraphs: Delivering a notice of appeal “stays, until the disposition of the appeal, any provision of the order for the payment of money, except a provision that awards support or enforces a support order.” When an order is stayed, “no steps may be taken under the order or for its enforcement,” except by order of a judge of the appeal court or as the rules otherwise provide. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 63.01 (1), r. 63.03 (1))

An appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment “does not stay the default judgment”, but it may be stayed by order. A judge of the appeal court may also order that the automatic stay does not apply. An order may be stayed “on such terms as are just” by the court that made it or by a judge of the appeal court. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 63.01 (2), (5), r. 63.02 (1))

sections.heading: Family cases: which court and which rules
paragraphs: An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from “a final order of a judge of the Family Court made only under a provision of an Act or regulation of Ontario”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1) (a.1))

For family appeals to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, including where leave is required, “Rules 61, 62 and 63 of the Rules of Civil Procedure apply with necessary changes”, including changes the rule sets out, such as different time periods in an appeal in a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (1), (2))

Rule 38 of the Family Law Rules sets out its own steps for appeals from an order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice under provisions such as section 48 of the Family Law Act and section 73 of the Children's Law Reform Act. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (4))

A final order of a Superior Court judge made on a first appeal from certain Ontario Court of Justice orders (under the Change of Name Act, the Children's Law Reform Act except sections 59 and 60, or section 6 of the Marriage Act) “may be appealed to the Court of Appeal only with leave from the Court of Appeal, as provided in the rules of court.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1.1), (1.2))

sections.heading: Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice
paragraphs: To appeal a final order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice under a provision listed in rule 38 (4), a party serves a notice of appeal (Form 38) “within 30 days after the date of the order or decision being appealed from”. It goes to every other party affected by or entitled to appeal, the clerk of the court that made the order and, in some child protection appeals, certain other persons. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (4), (5))
The notice of appeal is filed “within 10 days after serving the notice of appeal”. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (5))

For a temporary order, the notice of appeal is served “within seven days after the date of the temporary order.” In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, the time for appealing a temporary order is 30 days. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (6), (7))

The notice of appeal states “the order that the appellant wants the appeal court to make and the legal grounds for the appeal.” At the hearing, “no grounds other than the ones stated in the notice of appeal may be argued unless the court gives permission.” (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (10), (11))

If a transcript is needed, the appellant files proof it was ordered “within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal”. Outside child protection cases, the appellant's appeal record and factum are due within 60 days after notice that the evidence was transcribed, or within 30 days of filing the notice of appeal if no transcript is needed. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (12), (21))
